newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Ex-rebel says he regrets giving up arms.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ex-rebel says he regrets giving up arms.

text.p: Tribal rebels in Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts who gave up arms on government assurances of a normal life say they were duped.

"I feel cheated. I regret my decision to dissociate from the Shanti Bahini (peace force)," said Pradip Kumar Chakma, a former guerrilla commander in Chittagong Hill Tracts, scene of the 23-year tribal insurgency.
The Shanti Bahini began fighting in 1973 after Bangladesh rejected its demand for political autonomy in the 5,500 sq-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts, which border India and Burma.
The Shantis say the picturesque Hill Tracts, rich in forest resources, are their tribal homeland. They want some 300,000 Bengali-speaking settlers to be expelled.
The Bangladesh government rejects this and wants all the tribal peoples, including the Shantis, to live side-by-side with the Bengalis as good neighbours.
In return, the government would undertake massive development projects in the Hill Tracts and offer special privileges to the tribespeople in jobs, education and social security.
However, civil and military officials in Rangamati, one of three Hill Tracts districts, say that if too much is done for the tribal people, this might trigger a Bengali backlash.
"Nothing should be done unevenly for an indefinite period...because it could inflame settlers' anger and trigger a backlash," one army officer told Reuters last week.
Pradip Kumar has a different view. "The insurgency is being fanned by the government's broken promises, and a failure to give protection to those willing to give up arms," he said.
Pradip joined the Shanti Bahini in 1978 and surrendered in 1985 along with 232 others, responding to a government amnesty.
They were promised land to build homes and for farming, plus jobs, money to start a business and other benefits under the terms of the anmesty.
"But only six of us have got jobs. Others are just wandering the streets, their families are starving," Pradip said.
"Moreover, several ex-guerrillas have been killed by the Shantis as traitors...while others may be within the range of their guns," he said. "But the government and army have failed to protect them."
Pradip, in his mid-30s, said one his comrades had been shot and killed in May, leaving his family to beg. "We didn't come back for this. Sometimes I regret the decision.
"We still have the training...and some of us may be willing to rejoin the Shanti Bahini," he said.
Officials say the government has done what it could with its limited resources, and accused the ex-rebels of asking too much.
"We have thousands of unemployed Bengalis who were brought to the Hill Tracts by the government, but we could not give them jobs," one Hill Tracts official said.
"They are often attacked and killed by the rebels. They need security just as badly," he said.
Pradip recalled his association with the Shanti Bahini, made up of mostly Chakma tribesmen.
"Once I was severely tortured by the army for doing nothing," he said. "They made my life unbearable in the Hill Tracts. They suspected me of being a Shanti Bahini agent.
"I decided to flee and joined the Shantis," he said. "I was taken to a camp across the border in India and given full-length guerrilla training. Then I received arms and went to combat."
At least one ex-guerrilla appeared to be satisfied in his new role.
"Every man wants his right. I joined the Shanti Bahini for my rights, the rights of my people," said Rabindra Lal Chakma, now chairman of the Rangamati Local Council.
"Later I realised that the rebels are somewhat misguided... I had difference of opinion with my commanders and decided to come back," he told Reuters at his office recently.
"I was the first Shanti Bahini guerrilla to return. Some 1,200 others followed me in phases. The hill people have many grievances and expectations...but these can be realised without guns," he said.
